about.bio-text-1: I'm Tony Owen Peterson (TOP), a Seattle-based design leader specializing in prototyping and interaction design. I spent the last decade at Microsoft designing, mentoring, presenting, developing, deploying, collaborating, and cultivating fun across many different teams and orgs.
about.bio-text-2: I love being part of a creative team, whether I'm leading or collaborating to bring complex and sometimes wacky ideas to life. I continue to work in siloed ambiguity as a freelancer but have years of experience leading medium sized creative teams. Do you have a wacky idea you'd like me to help you bring to life?
about.bio-text-3: It's a role that looks at the big picture of how people interact with technology. Think of it as a problem-solver who also happens to have deep technical and visual skills. I bridge the gap between understanding what people actually need, designing a beautiful solution, and ensuring it can realistically be built in the real world. I care about both the aesthetics and the underlying logic, ensuring every experience is intuitive, seamless, and packed with delightful surprises.

projects.title: Shop in 3D
projects.hook:
Microsoft 3D Product Portal

The global pandemic killed the Microsoft Store, leaving a massive void in our customer journey. You cannot feel premium build quality through a screen, and relying on a static 2D image gallery is about as premium as a dial-up modem. We set out to hand the controls back to the user with a fully interactive digital experience that let them explore the hardware on their own terms. It was a wildly ambitious pivot, which meant I had to prototype the hell out of it to get the hard data and user feedback needed to prove it wasn't just a pipe dream.
projects.hustle: Being one of only two UX designers, and the sole prototyper, meant my hands were in every phase of this project, from early concepts to the final pitch. My real mission was taking the team's lofty vision and hammering it into a high-fidelity, fully interactive prototype. I essentially had to build a bulletproof blueprint so the external dev agency wouldn't have to guess how to actually build the customer-facing tool.
projects.hype: Originally built just to help sales associates run remote demos, it launched to the public in April 2021. Since then, it has successfully enriched engagement with tens of thousands of enthusiastic customers.

projects.hype: The highlight of the project was dropping our alpha build in front of hundreds of middle school students during a coding day challenge. We let our exact target demographic break the game and give us the unfiltered feedback we needed to refine it.

projects.title: Picchu
projects.hook:
Hey Microsoft! Let's align

Before the Microsoft Web Framework existed, the company's web landscape was a fragmented patchwork. Properties like windows.com and office.com were independent silos with unique component libraries and conflicting brand guidelines. We desperately needed a central point of truth to align the entire organization.
projects.hustle: The ecosystem was so disconnected that users were regularly getting stranded on isolated pages without a route back home. As the lead UX designer, I spearheaded the 'United Header Footer' initiative to unify the chaos. I helped develop the consistent navigation architecture that still spans the microsoft.com umbrella today.
projects.behind-the-scenes: With the 'bread' of the sandwich in place (UHF), our subsequent endeavor was to ensure that every contributor adhered to the right 'ingredients' and refrain from making 'sandwiches' out of breakfast cereal. This phase demanded meticulous consideration of the latest web technology, adherence to accessibility standards, and compatibility with various browsers. Designers sought guidance on image selection, dimensions, style guidance, fonts, colors, and brand voice alignment, while developers craved code and the knowledge to deploy it effectively. Picchu was conceived as a comprehensive portal, meticulously designed to cater to the unique requirements of both groups, streamlining their workflows without overwhelming them.
projects.hype: After months of relentless design, prototyping, and testing, we birthed a fully functional web framework. It gave developers the code they craved and designers the strict brand guardrails they needed, finally bringing the entire company into alignment.

Rebranding an entire organization is always a massive undertaking, but doing it for a church requires a completely different level of nuance. I was tasked with developing a new logo and visual language, alongside a compelling video to cast the vision to the congregation.
projects.hustle: This project was an absolute juggling act. I served as the director, editor, motion graphics artist, storyboarder, and scriptwriter, managing the entire production pipeline to ensure we delivered a beautiful, cohesive rebrand.
projects.tools:
Tools I used

  • Figma - For UI/UX design
  • VS Code - For development
  • Adobe Creative Suite - For asset creation
  • Git - For version control
projects.did-you-know: Gestalt principles of visual perception explain how humans group similar elements, recognize patterns, and simplify complex images in UX.

projects.title: Great Lakes Church Signage
projects.hook:
GLC Interior Signage Overhaul

We had three months to completely overhaul the interior signage across two separate campus locations. The goal was to build a foolproof wayfinding system so visitors could navigate the auditoriums, cafes, and kids areas without getting lost.
projects.hustle: I designed the entire environmental graphics suite, translating complex wayfinding needs into clear, beautiful visual communication. I then managed the print liaison duties and physically installed the artwork onto the walls.
projects.hype: The result? Happy visitors and a flawless navigation experience.
projects.tools:
Tools I used

  • Figma - For UI/UX design
  • VS Code - For development
  • Adobe Creative Suite - For asset creation
  • Git - For version control
projects.did-you-know: The aesthetic-usability effect suggests that users often perceive aesthetically pleasing designs as more usable.

projects.title: #staymarried
projects.hook:
From Blog to Movement: The #staymarried Story

What started in 2012 as a humble passion project blog by my partner Michelle and myself quickly evolved into a massive, thriving community.
projects.hustle: I designed every single piece of social marketing that fueled the movement. I built the infographics, charts, and visual stories that resonated so deeply with our audience that they eventually ended up being utilized by professional couples counselors.
projects.hype: The project exploded into a fully fledged brand featuring a podcast and a published book with over 100,000 copies sold. It generated millions of views and sparked countless healthy conversations.
projects.tools:
Tools I used

  • Figma - For UI/UX design
  • VS Code - For development
  • Adobe Creative Suite - For asset creation
  • Git - For version control
projects.did-you-know: Iterative design processes, where solutions are continuously prototyped and tested, dramatically reduce the risk of product failure.

projects.title: Eco Packaging Concept
projects.hook:
From Trash to Treasure: The Cardboard Lamp

As a UX designer on the Store team, I helped tackle the massive environmental impact of our hardware packaging. We came up with a brilliant concept to prevent Surface Notebook shipping boxes from immediately hitting the landfill: repurpose the cardboard into a DIY origami lamp.
projects.hustle: I brought the concept to life by designing and animating a step-by-step video guide. It beautifully illustrated the transformation from a piece of trash into a functional, stylish light fixture, proving that sustainable design can be genuinely fun.
projects.tools:
Tools I used

  • Figma - For UI/UX design
  • VS Code - For development
  • Adobe Creative Suite - For asset creation
  • Git - For version control
projects.did-you-know: A seamless omni-channel UX approach ensures users have a consistent experience across different devices and touchpoints.

projects.title: Mailers & Invites
projects.hook:
Rebranding the Church Experience

Reaching people who are deeply skeptical of attending church requires throwing out the traditional religious playbook. Our goal was to design a massive outreach campaign that explicitly appealed to a demographic that would normally throw a church mailer straight into the recycling bin.
projects.hustle: I designed high-quality physical invites and executed a direct mail campaign targeting 50,000 local addresses. I strictly avoided alienating language and focused on a 'transparently un-weird' visual strategy to normalize the experience.
projects.hype: The fresh approach successfully broke down long-standing visual barriers and drove measurable engagement from a highly skeptical target audience.
projects.tools:
Tools I used

  • Adobe Illustrator - For vector graphics and layout
  • Adobe Photoshop - For image manipulation
  • Adobe InDesign - For print preparation
projects.did-you-know: Cognitive load theory in UX dictates that simple, uncluttered interfaces help users process information and complete tasks faster.

games.title: Chick Collect
games.pitch: You play as a frantically dedicated mama bird on a mission. Your tiny chicks have wandered off and gotten themselves completely lost around the farm. It is your job to track them down, scoop them up, and safely guide your ever-growing, trailing flock back to the nest.
games.intention: I built this prototype to figure out two specific technical hurdles. First, I wanted to test out smooth fade transitions between different game states. Second, I really needed to wrestle with an array-based following mechanic. I wanted to figure out the exact logic of picking up interactive items and having them dynamically align to trail directly behind the player character.

games.title: Forest Adventure
games.pitch: You play as a young girl who wakes up in a mysterious forest with absolutely zero memory of who she is or how she got there. To piece together your identity and eventually find your way home, you have to explore the environment, collect scattered items, and solve a series of puzzles. Amnesia is tough, but wandering aimlessly until things make sense is a surprisingly solid strategy.
games.intention: I built this prototype to figure out how to recreate that classic, top-down adventure view from the original Zelda, just with much smoother, modern movement. I also used this project to test screen-to-screen sideways scrolling transitions. Beyond the camera mechanics, I needed to figure out the underlying logic for map teleportation when entering doors and wrap my head around building a basic inventory management system.

games.title: Identity Theft
games.pitch: You play as a master of disguise whose entire identity is dictated by whatever happens to be sitting on your head. Slap on a cowboy hat, and you are instantly a cowboy. Find a crown, and you are suddenly royalty. The core gameplay loop revolves around swapping headwear to solve puzzles and bypass stubborn NPCs. A guard is not going to let you out of your cell unless you look like a king, or perhaps another guard. Want access to the restricted kitchen? Better go track down that chef hat. It is a point and click puzzle game where your wardrobe is your security clearance.
games.intention: Pico-8 is famous for its classic directional pad and button controls, which means mouse-driven games are a rarity on the platform. While the engine absolutely has built-in mouse functionality, it is rarely the avenue developers choose. I built this prototype to step away from the keyboard and explore those lesser-used capabilities. I wanted to completely map out the cursor behaviors and understand the exact mechanics required to build a functional point and click system in an environment that usually defaults to a D-pad.

games.title: Turnip Head Balance
games.pitch: You play as Turnip Head, and your only goal is to stay upright. That is really the entire premise. The controls are stripped down to just left and right, and you are simply trying to maintain your balance for as long as possible.
games.intention: This is my most polished prototype to date. Instead of relying on traditional sprites and sprite sheets, the visuals are almost completely rendered using raw geometry. It also features a custom soundtrack I scored myself, based on the movie, which I am genuinely proud of. Technically, I built this to test out a balancing physics mechanic for a larger, WarioWare style game concept themed around 'Howl's Moving Castle'. This was designed to be one of the rapid-fire mini-games, and I needed to ensure the physics felt plausible and fun on their own before building out the rest of the castle.

games.title: Howls
games.pitch: Welcome to the main living area of the moving castle. You play as Howl, hanging out next to Calcifer, and your objective is to walk around and interact with various objects scattered across the room. Ultimately, this environment acts as the central hub, serving as a WarioWare style launcher designed to house and trigger all the other mini-games.
games.intention: My primary goal for building this specific room was to tackle complicated, multi-frame animated walking cycles. I also wanted to spend some serious time fussing with the camera logic, specifically locking the viewport directly onto the player character so the environment pans smoothly around them as they explore.

games.title: Tony's Breakout
games.pitch: It is traditional Breakout at its core. Keep the ball bouncing and smash every brick on the screen so you can progress to the next level. To keep things interesting, you can grab various power-ups that speed up the ball, multiply them into a chaotic swarm, or make them delightfully sticky.
games.intention: I followed a tutorial for this one, and it served as a fantastic exercise in pure game polish. I used it as a hands-on crash course to learn how to build particle systems, write simple arcade physics, and manage complex game states.

games.title: Graveyard Test
games.pitch: You play as a ghost wandering through a graveyard that is inexplicably covered in garbage. Your singular mission is to clean up the afterlife by picking up the trash and returning it to the proper bin. It is essentially a spooky sanitation job wrapped in a dark, atmospheric visual style.
games.intention: This prototype was born from a tutorial, and it is entirely responsible for sparking my interest in top-down adventure games. Mechanically, there is not much going on beyond the core visuals and basic screen-to-screen movement. However, this served as the alpha version that directly inspired the 'Forest Adventure' prototype, where I eventually doubled down on smooth camera transitions and built a proper inventory system.

games.title: Tony Shmup
games.pitch: You are in a spaceship, and you shoot aliens. That is the entire premise.
games.intention: Building a shoot 'em up is basically a game designer's rite of passage, and this prototype is my official contribution to the genre. I followed a tutorial to learn how to wire up classic shooting mechanics, manage game states, and program power moves. The main goal was just to get under the hood and feel out some authentic, old-school arcade mechanics.

games.title: Tony Pork
games.pitch: You play as a pig navigating a treacherous dungeon tower, climbing higher and higher with each floor. Along the way, you collect items and battle enemies, but since you are a pig, the loot is entirely food-themed. Prepare to wield weapons like a salami sword as you fight your way to the top in this highly enjoyable dungeon crawler.
games.intention: This prototype is based on an incredibly in-depth tutorial that served as a masterclass in game design concepts. My main goal was to explore grid-based movement and classic roguelike mechanics, specifically the turn-based system where enemies only move when you make a move. It was also a deep dive into pathfinding algorithms, teaching the NPCs how to calculate the most efficient route to hunt down the player. It was a fantastic exercise in bringing a high level of polish to a complex system.

games.title: Robo Farming
games.pitch: You play as an agricultural robot in a farming simulator reminiscent of Stardew Valley. The core loop is familiar: plant seeds, water your crops, reap the harvest, and sell your bounty to buy even more seeds. The catch is that every single action drains your battery level. You have to carefully manage your energy and plan your daily tasks before you completely run out of juice.
games.intention: I built this prototype by following a tutorial specifically to get a solid grasp on general farming game mechanics. It served as a highly practical way to learn how to build and manage in-game menus, track resources, and wire up a functional economic loop.
